sectionTitle: Changes of state and the particle model

specStatements.text: The density of a material is defined by the equation:
density, ρ, in kilograms per metre cubed, kg/m^3
volume, V, in metres cubed, m^3
The particle model can be used to explain
Students should be able to recognise/draw simple diagrams to model the difference between solids, liquids and gases.
Students should be able to explain the differences in density between the different states of matter in terms of the arrangement of atoms or molecules.

Required practical activity 5: use appropriate apparatus to make and record the measurements needed to determine the densities of regular and irregular solid objects and liquids. Volume should be determined from the dimensions of regularly shaped objects, and by a displacement technique for irregularly shaped objects. Dimensions to be measured using appropriate apparatus such as a ruler, micrometer or Vernier callipers.
AT skills covered by this practical activity: AT 1.
This practical activity also provides opportunities to develop WS and MS. Details of all skills are given in Key opportunities for skills development.
Students should be able to describe how, w hen substances change state (melt, freeze, boil, evaporate, condense or sublimate), mass is conserved.
Changes of state are physical changes which differ from chemical changes because the material recovers its original properties if the change is reversed.

scopeNotes.statement: Volume should be determined from the dimensions of regularly shaped objects, and by a displacement technique for irregularly shaped objects.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The two routes to a volume are kept separate exactly as the specification separates them. Regularly shaped objects are handled by measuring dimensions and calculating (c13, q09); irregularly shaped objects are handled only by displacement (c14, q10). No item asks a student to estimate the volume of an irregular object from its dimensions, and no item asks for a volume by any method the specification does not name, such as weighing in water or using a formula for an odd shape.

scopeNotes.statement: Dimensions to be measured using appropriate apparatus such as a ruler, micrometer or Vernier callipers.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Only the three named instruments are used for dimensions (c16, q12), and they are compared on the one basis the specification implies by listing them together: choosing apparatus appropriate to the size of the dimension. No reading technique beyond this - no Vernier scale arithmetic, no micrometer zero-error correction - is taught or tested, because the specification asks for appropriate apparatus, not for instrument theory.

scopeNotes.statement: AT skills covered by this practical activity: AT 1.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: This is a signpost to the apparatus and techniques list, not additional physics content, so it generates no questions of its own. It is honoured by keeping the practical material inside AT 1: using appropriate apparatus to make and record measurements of length, mass and volume accurately, and using those measurements to find the densities of solid and liquid objects (c13, c14, c15, c16). Nothing is drawn from any other AT statement.

scopeNotes.statement: This practical activity also provides opportunities to develop WS and MS. Details of all skills are given in Key opportunities for skills development.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: This statement points to skills listed elsewhere in the specification and adds no physics content, so it is discharged rather than taught, and carries no questions. The mathematical skills it flags are exercised only through the density content itself - rearranging ρ = m/V (c02, q02), converting g/cm³ to kg/m³ (c06, q05) and calculating a volume from three dimensions (c05, q04). No WS or MS skill is invented here, and none is assessed apart from the density work of 4.3.1.1.

concepts.definition: Density is the mass of a material per unit volume. The specification defines it by the equation density = mass / volume. A material has a high density when a large mass is packed into a small volume. Density is a property of the material itself: it does not depend on how much of the material you have.

In words, density = mass / volume. In symbols, ρ = m/V, where ρ is the density, m is the mass and V is the volume. This is an equation students are expected to recall and apply, and to rearrange as m = ρV or V = m/ρ.

In the equation as the specification states it, density, ρ, is in kilograms per metre cubed, kg/m³. The unit follows directly from the equation: a mass in kilograms divided by a volume in metres cubed gives kilograms per metre cubed.
Mass, m, is in kilograms, kg. Mass is measured on a balance. Weight is a force measured in newtons and must not be substituted into ρ = m/V in place of mass.

Volume, V, is in metres cubed, m³. For a regularly shaped solid the volume is calculated from its measured dimensions (for a cuboid, length x width x height). For an irregularly shaped solid it is found by a displacement technique.

Densities are often quoted in g/cm³, but the specification's unit is kg/m³. Since 1 g = 0.001 kg and 1 cm³ = 0.000001 m³, a density of 1 g/cm³ is 1000 kg/m³. To convert from g/cm³ to kg/m³, multiply by 1000. Water is about 1.0 g/cm³, that is 1000 kg/m³.

A model that treats a substance as being made of atoms or molecules whose arrangement, separation and movement differ from one state of matter to another. The specification uses the particle model to explain the different states of matter and differences in density.
In a solid the particles are packed closely together, touching one another in a regular arrangement, and vibrate about fixed positions. A solid keeps its own shape and its own volume.
In a liquid the particles are still close together and touching, but they are arranged randomly and can move past one another. A liquid keeps its own volume but takes the shape of its container.

In a gas the particles are far apart compared with the size of the particles themselves, arranged randomly, and move quickly in all directions. A gas has no fixed shape and no fixed volume; it fills its container.

concepts.term: Simple particle diagrams of the three states
concepts.definition: A solid is drawn as circles touching in a regular, ordered pattern. A liquid is drawn as circles touching but jumbled, filling the lower part of the container. A gas is drawn as a few widely separated circles spread through the whole container. The circles are the same size in all three diagrams, because the particles themselves do not change.

concepts.term: Explaining differences in density from the arrangement of particles
concepts.definition: The particles of a given substance have the same mass in every state, so a difference in density must come from a difference in the volume the same particles occupy. Solids and liquids have similar densities because in both the particles are touching. A gas is very much less dense, commonly by a factor of about a thousand, because the same particles are spread through a far larger volume.

concepts.term: Determining the density of a regular solid
concepts.definition: Measure the mass of the object on a balance. Measure its dimensions with appropriate apparatus and calculate the volume from those dimensions (for a cuboid, length x width x height). Then calculate density using ρ = m/V.

concepts.term: Displacement technique for an irregular solid
concepts.definition: The volume of an irregularly shaped object is found by displacement. Lower the object, fully submerged, into a measuring cylinder holding a known volume of water and record the new reading; the volume of the object is the increase in the reading. Alternatively, lower it into a displacement can filled to the spout and measure the water that overflows in a measuring cylinder. Its mass is measured separately on a balance.

concepts.term: Determining the density of a liquid
concepts.definition: Measure the mass of an empty measuring cylinder on a balance. Pour the liquid in, record its volume, and measure the mass again. The mass of the liquid is the difference between the two balance readings, and the density is that mass divided by the measured volume.

The specification names a ruler, a micrometer and Vernier callipers. The instrument is chosen to suit the size of the dimension being measured: a ruler (resolution about 1 mm) for a block a few centimetres across, Vernier callipers (about 0.1 mm) for smaller objects, and a micrometer (about 0.01 mm) for very small dimensions such as the diameter of a wire.

The specification names six changes of state: melting, freezing, boiling, evaporating, condensing and sublimating. Melting is solid to liquid and freezing is liquid to solid; boiling and evaporating are liquid to gas and condensing is gas to liquid; sublimating is solid straight to gas.

concepts.term: Conservation of mass in a change of state
concepts.definition: When a substance changes state, mass is conserved: no particles are created or destroyed, so the mass after the change is equal to the mass before it. If a balance reading falls while a liquid boils away, the mass has left the container as a gas; it has not been destroyed.

A change of state is a physical change. It differs from a chemical change because the material recovers its original properties if the change is reversed. No new substance is produced; only the arrangement and the movement of the particles change.

misconceptions.question: A large lump of expanded polystyrene has a bigger mass than a small steel ball bearing. Which has the greater density?
misconceptions.correct: The steel. Density is mass per unit volume, not mass on its own. The steel packs far more mass into each cubic metre, so its density is about 7800 kg/m³ against roughly 20 kg/m³ for the polystyrene.
misconceptions.misconception: The polystyrene, because it is heavier - the heavier object must be the denser one.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In everyday speech 'heavy' and 'dense' are used interchangeably, and students meet mass long before they meet density. Comparing two objects of very different sizes hides the fact that density is a ratio, so only the top of the ratio is noticed.
misconceptions.correction: Always compare equal volumes. Ask which would be heavier: a cubic centimetre of steel or a cubic centimetre of polystyrene. Once the volume is fixed, the comparison of mass is a comparison of density.

misconceptions.question: A 2 kg aluminium block is cut exactly in half. What is the density of each half?
misconceptions.correct: Unchanged, about 2700 kg/m³. The mass halves and the volume halves, so the ratio mass / volume is the same. Density is a property of the material, not of the size of the sample.
misconceptions.misconception: Cutting the block in half must halve the density, because there is only half as much aluminium left.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Density is met through the equation, and the equation contains mass, which obviously halves. Students track the numerator and forget that the denominator halves at the same time.
misconceptions.correction: Work the numbers through: if m and V both halve, m / V is unchanged. Reinforce that every piece of a pure material, however small, has the same density.

misconceptions.question: A liquid has a mass of 2.0 kg and a volume of 0.0025 m³. Which way round does the calculation go?
misconceptions.correct: Density = mass / volume = 2.0 / 0.0025 = 800 kg/m³. Mass is divided by volume, never the other way round.
misconceptions.misconception: It does not matter which way round you divide; you just divide the bigger number by the smaller one to keep the answer tidy.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Dividing a small number into a large one feels wrong to students, and awkward decimals such as 0.0025 encourage them to flip the calculation so the arithmetic looks friendlier.
misconceptions.correction: Anchor the order to the unit. Density is in kilograms per metre cubed, and 'per' means divided by, so kilograms go on top and metres cubed underneath. The unit tells you the order every time.

misconceptions.question: Is the density of a 3.0 kg block of volume 0.0020 m³ found by multiplying or dividing?
misconceptions.correct: By dividing: 3.0 / 0.0020 = 1500 kg/m³. The equation is ρ = m/V.
misconceptions.misconception: You multiply mass by volume, because a bigger object with a bigger volume must have more density in it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students who half-remember the equation reach for multiplication because it is easier, and because 'more stuff means more density' sounds reasonable when density and amount have not been separated.
misconceptions.correction: Check the answer against the unit and against a known material. Multiplying gives a number in kg m³, which is not a density unit at all, and gives water a value nothing like 1000 kg/m³.

misconceptions.question: A student measures a block with a newton-meter and records 5.9 N. Can that value be used in ρ = m/V?
misconceptions.correct: No. The equation needs mass in kilograms, measured on a balance. The 5.9 N is a weight, which is a force in newtons.
misconceptions.misconception: Mass and weight are the same thing, so a reading in newtons can go straight into the density equation.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everyday language uses 'weight' for what a balance shows, and both quantities increase together for a given object, so the distinction feels like fussy vocabulary rather than a real difference.
misconceptions.correction: The specification is explicit: mass, m, in kilograms, kg. A newton-meter measures force. Insist on a balance for mass, and keep newtons out of ρ = m/V.

misconceptions.question: Copper has a density of 8.96 g/cm³. What is that in kg/m³?
misconceptions.correct: 8960 kg/m³. Changing the unit changes the number: 1 g/cm³ is 1000 kg/m³, so multiply by 1000.
misconceptions.misconception: The number stays as 8.96 - only the label after it changes when you rewrite the unit.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students see unit changes as relabelling rather than rescaling, and because both unit strings contain a mass unit over a volume unit the two look equivalent at a glance.
misconceptions.correction: Use water as the check. Water is 1.0 g/cm³ and 1000 kg/m³, and the same substance cannot have two different numbers unless the unit changes the scale.

misconceptions.question: To convert 2.7 g/cm³ into kg/m³, do you multiply or divide by 1000?
misconceptions.correct: Multiply: 2.7 g/cm³ = 2700 kg/m³. The volume unit grows by a factor of 1 000 000 while the mass unit only grows by 1000, so the number gets larger.
misconceptions.misconception: Grams are smaller than kilograms, so you must divide by 1000, giving 0.0027 kg/m³.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Only the mass part of the unit is converted. The cubic centimetre to cubic metre step is invisible, and it is the larger factor of the two.
misconceptions.correction: Convert both parts. 1 g = 0.001 kg and 1 cm³ = 0.000001 m³, so 1 g/cm³ = 0.001 / 0.000001 = 1000 kg/m³. Sense-check the size: aluminium at 0.0027 kg/m³ would be lighter than air.

misconceptions.question: A cube of side 0.20 m has a mass of 54 kg. What volume goes into the density equation?
misconceptions.correct: 0.20 x 0.20 x 0.20 = 0.008 m³, giving a density of 6750 kg/m³.
misconceptions.misconception: You divide the mass by the length of the side, or by the area of one face, because that is the measurement you took.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The measured quantity is a length, so it is the number students reach for. Working in three dimensions is an extra step that is easy to drop, especially when the side length is less than one and cubing makes the number smaller.
misconceptions.correction: Label every number with its unit before dividing. Only m³ underneath gives kg/m³ on top; dividing by a length gives kg/m, which is not a density.

misconceptions.question: When ice melts to water, do the water molecules become bigger?
misconceptions.correct: No. The molecules are unchanged. What changes is how they are arranged and how they move; the same molecules occupy a slightly different volume.
misconceptions.misconception: Particles swell up when a substance melts or boils, and that is why a gas takes up so much more room than a liquid.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Diagrams of a gas often use larger or more spread-out circles, and everyday talk of things 'expanding' is applied to the particles themselves rather than to the spaces between them.
misconceptions.correction: Draw all three states with identical circles and change only the spacing and pattern. Expansion is extra space between particles, never bigger particles.

misconceptions.question: In a liquid, how far apart are the particles compared with a solid?
misconceptions.correct: About the same. Liquid particles are still touching; they are simply jumbled and free to move past one another. That is why a liquid has a density close to that of the solid.
misconceptions.misconception: Liquid particles are spaced out about halfway between a solid and a gas, so a liquid is far less dense than the solid.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Textbook diagrams often exaggerate the gaps in liquids to show that the particles can move, and the sequence solid, liquid, gas suggests spacing increases in equal steps.
misconceptions.correction: Compare real values: ice is about 920 kg/m³, water 1000 kg/m³, steam about 0.6 kg/m³. The huge jump comes at boiling, which tells you the big change in spacing happens there.

misconceptions.question: How should the particles in a solid be drawn?
misconceptions.correct: Touching one another in a regular, ordered pattern, with no gaps between them.
misconceptions.misconception: A solid should be drawn as a neat grid of particles with clear spaces between them, because there is space inside every material.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students draw a lattice to show order and leave gaps so the pattern is easy to see. The gaps then get read as a physical feature of the solid.
misconceptions.correction: Marking a diagram of a solid requires the particles to be touching as well as regular. Order and close packing are two separate points, and both must appear.

misconceptions.question: Why is steam so much less dense than liquid water?
misconceptions.correct: Because the same molecules are spread through a far greater volume. Each molecule is identical to a molecule in the liquid; there are simply far fewer of them in each cubic metre.
misconceptions.misconception: Gas particles must be smaller and lighter than liquid particles, otherwise the gas could not be so light.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Density is being explained by a property of the individual particle rather than by their spacing, which is the only thing the particle model actually changes between states.
misconceptions.correction: Ask where the extra particles would have gone. Boil 1 kg of water and you get 1 kg of steam, made of exactly the same molecules; only the volume has changed.

misconceptions.question: Is a substance always denser as a solid than as a liquid?
misconceptions.correct: For most substances, yes, because the particles pack slightly more closely in the solid. Water is the well-known exception: ice floats because its molecules are held in a more open arrangement than in liquid water, so ice is less dense.
misconceptions.misconception: The solid form of any substance must be denser than the liquid, so ice ought to sink in water.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The rule that solids are denser than liquids is learned as absolute, and the everyday sight of floating ice is filed away separately instead of being used to test the rule.
misconceptions.correction: Keep the explanation in terms of arrangement. Density follows from how closely the particles are packed, and in ice the arrangement is more open than in liquid water, so the usual order is reversed.

misconceptions.question: A measuring cylinder holds 40 cm³ of water. A stone is lowered in and the level rises to 65 cm³. What is the volume of the stone?
misconceptions.correct: 25 cm³, the increase in the reading. The stone displaces its own volume of water.
misconceptions.misconception: The volume of the stone is 65 cm³, because that is the reading on the cylinder once the stone is in.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The final reading is the number the student has just read, and it feels like the answer. The starting volume of water is treated as part of the apparatus rather than as part of the measurement.
misconceptions.correction: Always record both readings and subtract. The water that was already there has not become part of the stone.

misconceptions.question: An empty measuring cylinder has a mass of 85 g. With 50 cm³ of oil in it the total mass is 129 g. What is the density of the oil?
misconceptions.correct: 0.88 g/cm³. The oil alone has a mass of 129 - 85 = 44 g, and 44 / 50 = 0.88 g/cm³.
misconceptions.misconception: Divide 129 g by 50 cm³, because 129 g is what the balance reads when the oil is being measured.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The balance reading is taken as the mass of the liquid. Once the cylinder is on the balance it stops being seen as an object with a mass of its own.
misconceptions.correction: Either subtract the mass of the empty cylinder or zero (tare) the balance with the empty cylinder on it. Sense-check the answer: an oil of 2.6 g/cm³ would be denser than glass.

misconceptions.question: A copper wire is about 0.4 mm across. Should it be measured with a ruler?
misconceptions.correct: No. A ruler resolves to about 1 mm, which is larger than the diameter itself. A micrometer, resolving to about 0.01 mm, is the appropriate instrument.
misconceptions.misconception: A ruler is fine for anything you can see, so 0.4 mm can just be estimated between the millimetre marks.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Rulers are the familiar instrument and estimating between marks feels like good practice. The idea that an instrument has a resolution, and that the measurement is worthless below it, is newer and less concrete.
misconceptions.correction: Compare the resolution with the measurement. An uncertainty of about 0.5 mm on a 0.4 mm diameter is larger than the quantity being measured; with a micrometer it is around 1 per cent.

misconceptions.question: Does it matter which length-measuring instrument is used, as long as it reads in millimetres?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. A ruler, Vernier callipers and a micrometer resolve to roughly 1 mm, 0.1 mm and 0.01 mm, so the choice must suit the size of the dimension being measured.
misconceptions.misconception: Any instrument will do, because they all measure length in the same unit and so give the same answer.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Instruments are grouped by what they measure rather than by how finely they measure it, and the unit on the scale is mistaken for the precision of the reading.
misconceptions.correction: Set the instrument against the object. Use a ruler for a block of a few centimetres, callipers for smaller objects, and a micrometer for a wire or a thin sheet.

misconceptions.question: A pan of water is boiled dry on a balance and the reading falls to zero. Has mass been destroyed?
misconceptions.correct: No. The water has left the pan as steam. Mass is conserved: the water molecules still exist, but they are now in the air rather than on the balance.
misconceptions.misconception: Boiling uses the water up, so that mass really has gone - the heat destroys it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The balance provides direct evidence that seems to settle the question, and a gas that disperses invisibly stops feeling like a substance at all.
misconceptions.correction: Follow the particles, not the balance. Repeat the change in a sealed container and the reading does not change, because nothing has left the system.

misconceptions.question: A sealed bottle of water is put in a freezer. Does its mass change as the water freezes?
misconceptions.correct: No. Mass is conserved in a change of state. The ice takes up slightly more volume than the water did, so the density falls, but the mass is exactly the same.
misconceptions.misconception: The ice must be heavier, because it takes up more room than the water did.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Volume and mass are not yet separated, so anything that gets bigger is assumed to have gained matter. Freezing water is the everyday example where the two clearly come apart.
misconceptions.correction: Keep mass and volume separate. Freezing changes only the arrangement of the molecules, so V goes up, m stays the same and ρ = m/V goes down.

misconceptions.question: Does the water vapour that leaves a puddle have any mass?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. A gas is made of the same particles as the liquid, so it has mass. Weighing a sealed flask before and after a liquid evaporates inside it shows no change.
misconceptions.misconception: Gases have no mass at all - you cannot weigh air, and steam just floats away.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Gases are invisible, they rise, and nothing is felt when a hand passes through them, so students treat 'no weight you can feel' as 'no mass'.
misconceptions.correction: Point to evidence that gases have mass: a sealed container of an evaporating liquid keeps the same reading throughout, because the particles are still inside it.

misconceptions.question: Water is boiled to make steam. Is that a chemical change?
misconceptions.correct: No. It is a physical change. No new substance is made; cooling the steam gives back water with all of its original properties.
misconceptions.misconception: Steam is a new substance with different properties from water, so boiling must be a chemical change.
misconceptions.whyItArises: A change in appearance is read as a change of substance, and the three states are often given different names, which makes them sound like different materials.
misconceptions.correction: Apply the specification's test: reverse the change and see whether the original properties come back. Condense the steam and it is water again, so nothing new was made.

misconceptions.question: Is every change that can be reversed a physical change?
misconceptions.correct: Not necessarily. What makes a change of state physical is that the material recovers its original properties when the change is reversed, so no new substance was ever made.
misconceptions.misconception: Physical changes are the reversible ones and chemical changes can never be reversed, so anything reversible must be physical.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Reversible means physical' is an easy rule to remember, and most classroom chemical changes are hard to undo, which appears to confirm it.
misconceptions.correction: State the test the way the specification does: the material recovers its original properties if the change is reversed. It is the recovery of the same material, not the mere fact of reversal, that marks the change as physical.

mcqs.stem: How is the density of a material defined?

options.text: The mass of the material divided by its volume.
options.rationale: This is the definition the specification gives: density = mass / volume, or ρ = m/V.

options.text: The volume of the material divided by its mass.
options.rationale: The division is reversed. Students who are unsure of the order divide the larger number by the smaller one, which for most solids means volume last.

options.text: The mass of the material multiplied by its volume.
options.rationale: Half-remembering the equation as a product. It also fails the unit test: multiplying gives kg m³, not kg/m³.

options.text: The mass of the material, whatever its volume is.
options.rationale: Density is taken to be the same thing as mass, which is why a large heavy object is assumed to be the dense one.

mcqs.stem: A liquid has a density of 800 kg/m³ and a mass of 2.0 kg. What is its volume?

options.text: 400 m³
options.rationale: Density has been divided by mass (800 / 2.0) instead of mass by density.
Rearranging ρ = m/V gives V = m/ρ = 2.0 / 800 = 0.0025 m³.
Mass has been multiplied by density (2.0 x 800), the same error as writing ρ = m x V.
The rearrangement is right but the decimal place is out by a factor of ten, a common slip when dividing by 800.

mcqs.stem: Which unit does the specification use for density?

options.text: g/cm³
options.rationale: A real density unit, and the one often printed in data books, but not the unit the specification uses; the two differ by a factor of 1000.

options.text: m³/kg
options.rationale: The equation has been inverted, so the unit is inverted with it.

options.text: kg/m³
options.rationale: The specification states density, ρ, in kilograms per metre cubed, kg/m³.

options.text: kg/m²
options.rationale: Comes from using an area rather than a volume underneath the mass.

mcqs.stem: A solid cube of side 0.20 m has a mass of 54 kg. What is its density?

options.text: 270 kg/m³
options.rationale: The mass has been divided by the side length (54 / 0.20) rather than by the volume.

options.text: 1350 kg/m³
options.rationale: The mass has been divided by the area of one face (54 / 0.04), stopping at two dimensions instead of three.

options.text: 0.43 kg/m³
options.rationale: Mass has been multiplied by volume (54 x 0.008) instead of divided by it.

options.text: 6750 kg/m³

mcqs.stem: Aluminium has a density of 2.7 g/cm³. What is this in kg/m³?

options.text: 2700 kg/m³
options.rationale: 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³, so 2.7 g/cm³ = 2.7 x 1000 = 2700 kg/m³.
Only the mass unit has been converted, by dividing by 1000. A density below that of air should look wrong for a metal.

options.text: 2.7 kg/m³
options.rationale: The unit has been rewritten without rescaling the number, as though the two units were the same size.

options.text: 27 kg/m³
options.rationale: The right direction but the wrong factor: multiplied by 10 rather than by 1000.

mcqs.stem: Which description matches a correct simple particle diagram of a solid?

options.text: Particles evenly spaced in a grid, with gaps in between them.
options.rationale: The order is right but the particles are drawn apart. Students leave gaps so the pattern shows up clearly.

options.text: Particles touching each other in a regular, ordered pattern.
options.rationale: A solid is close-packed and ordered; both features must appear in the diagram.

options.text: Particles touching one another but jumbled, not in a pattern.
options.rationale: This is the diagram for a liquid: close-packed but disordered.

options.text: Particles well spread out and moving quickly in all directions.
options.rationale: This is the diagram for a gas, chosen when the states are ordered by movement rather than by arrangement.

mcqs.stem: Why is the density of a gas far lower than the density of the same substance as a liquid?

options.text: The particles in a gas are lighter than those in a liquid.
options.rationale: Density is explained by a property of the particle instead of by its spacing; boiling cannot change what a molecule is.

options.text: Each particle grows bigger when the liquid becomes a gas.
options.rationale: Expansion is attributed to the particles rather than to the space between them, an idea reinforced by loosely drawn diagrams.

options.text: The same particles are spread through a much larger volume.
options.rationale: Mass per particle is unchanged, so the drop in density comes entirely from the increase in volume.

options.text: The particles move faster, so gravity pulls on them less.
options.rationale: Speed is linked to weight. Density is mass per unit volume and does not depend on how fast the particles travel.

mcqs.stem: A block of solid wax melts. The mass does not change, but the liquid wax takes up slightly more volume. What happens to the density?

options.text: It stays the same, because exactly the same particles are present.
options.rationale: Conservation of mass is applied to density. Density can change even though mass does not, because the volume has changed.

options.text: It falls a long way, because liquid particles are far apart.
options.rationale: Liquid spacing is overestimated. Melting changes the arrangement, not the fact that the particles touch.

options.text: It falls, because each particle becomes larger as the wax melts.
options.rationale: The right direction for the wrong reason: the particles are unchanged and only their spacing alters.

options.text: It falls slightly, because the particles are a little further apart.
options.rationale: With m fixed and V slightly larger, ρ = m/V is slightly smaller. Solids and liquids have similar densities because the particles stay in contact.

mcqs.stem: A student is finding the density of a rectangular metal block. Which measurements are needed?

options.text: The mass on a balance, and the length, width and height.
options.rationale: The volume of a regularly shaped object is calculated from its dimensions, and the mass is measured on a balance.

options.text: The mass on a balance, and the area of its largest face.
options.rationale: Stops at two dimensions. An area divided into a mass gives kg/m², not a density.

options.text: The weight in newtons, and the length, width and height.
options.rationale: Weight is substituted for mass. The specification requires mass in kilograms, measured on a balance.

options.text: The mass on a balance, and the length of its longest side.
options.rationale: Only one dimension is taken, so the volume cannot be worked out for a block that is not a cube.

mcqs.stem: A measuring cylinder contains 40 cm³ of water. A stone of mass 60 g is lowered in and the level rises to 65 cm³. What is the density of the stone?

options.text: 0.92 g/cm³
options.rationale: The final reading of 65 cm³ has been used as the volume of the stone, without subtracting the water already there.

options.text: 2.4 g/cm³
options.rationale: The stone displaces 65 - 40 = 25 cm³ of water, so ρ = 60 / 25 = 2.4 g/cm³.

options.text: 1.5 g/cm³
options.rationale: The starting volume of 40 cm³ has been used, which is the volume of the water before the stone went in.

options.text: 0.42 g/cm³
options.rationale: Volume has been divided by mass (25 / 60) instead of mass by volume.

mcqs.stem: An empty measuring cylinder has a mass of 85 g. It is filled to the 50 cm³ mark with oil and the total mass is 129 g. What is the density of the oil?

options.text: 2.58 g/cm³
options.rationale: The whole balance reading of 129 g has been divided by the volume, counting the cylinder as if it were oil.

options.text: 1.14 g/cm³
options.rationale: The mass of oil is right but the division is the wrong way round (50 / 44).

options.text: 0.88 g/cm³
options.rationale: The oil alone has a mass of 129 - 85 = 44 g, so ρ = 44 / 50 = 0.88 g/cm³.

options.text: 1.70 g/cm³
options.rationale: The mass of the empty cylinder has been divided by the volume of the oil, mixing two unrelated measurements.

mcqs.stem: Which apparatus is most suitable for measuring the diameter of a copper wire about 0.4 mm across?

options.text: A ruler, because 0.4 mm can be judged between the marks.
options.rationale: A ruler resolves to about 1 mm, which is larger than the diameter being measured.

options.text: Any of the three, since they all measure a length in mm.
options.rationale: The unit on the scale is mistaken for the precision of the instrument.

options.text: Vernier callipers, which read to the nearest millimetre.
options.rationale: Callipers are named in the specification, but they read to about 0.1 mm, not 1 mm, and here a micrometer is the better choice.

options.text: A micrometer, which has a resolution of about 0.01 mm.
options.rationale: The resolution is far smaller than the diameter, so the percentage uncertainty is around 1 per cent.

mcqs.stem: A 200 g block of ice melts completely inside a sealed container. What is the mass of the water formed?

options.text: 200 g, because exactly the same particles are still there.
options.rationale: Mass is conserved in a change of state; melting rearranges the particles but does not create or destroy any.

options.text: Less than 200 g, because some of the ice is used up in melting.
options.rationale: Change of state is treated as consuming matter, in the way a fuel is consumed.

options.text: More than 200 g, because the water is denser than the ice was.
options.rationale: A change in density is read as a change in mass. Density changes here because the volume changes, not the mass.

options.text: 200 g at first, and then less as the water spreads itself out.
options.rationale: Spreading out is confused with losing mass; in a sealed container nothing can leave.

mcqs.stem: Water is boiled away in an open pan standing on a balance, and the reading falls. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The mass has been destroyed by the heat from the hotplate.
options.rationale: The falling reading is taken as direct evidence that matter can be destroyed by heating.

options.text: The steam has carried the mass out of the pan; none is lost.
options.rationale: Mass is conserved. The water molecules are now in the air, so they are no longer on the balance.

options.text: The water has become steam, and a gas has no mass at all.
options.rationale: Gases are invisible and cannot be felt, so students conclude they have no mass.

options.text: The mass has been turned into the energy needed for boiling.
options.rationale: Mass and energy are conflated. In a change of state, energy is transferred but no mass is converted.

mcqs.stem: Why is boiling water classed as a physical change rather than a chemical change?

options.text: Steam is a new substance, but the water can be made again.
options.rationale: Accepts that a new substance is formed, which would make it a chemical change; no new substance is made when water boils.

options.text: Reversing it is possible, and chemical changes are never reversible.
options.rationale: Reversibility alone is used as the test. What matters is that the same material comes back.

options.text: Cooling the steam gives back water with its original properties.
options.rationale: This is the specification's test: the material recovers its original properties if the change is reversed.

options.text: No energy at all is transferred to the water while it boils.
options.rationale: Energy transfer is assumed to mark a chemical change. Boiling needs a large energy transfer and is still physical.

mcqs.stem: Solid carbon dioxide sublimates in an open dish on a balance and the reading falls. Which explanation is correct?

options.text: The solid has been used up, so that mass no longer exists.
options.rationale: The change of state is treated as destroying matter rather than moving it.

options.text: A chemical reaction has turned the solid into a new gas.
options.rationale: Sublimation is a physical change: the carbon dioxide is the same substance in a different state.

options.text: Sublimation skips the liquid state, so some mass is missed.
options.rationale: Missing out a state is taken to mean missing out some matter; the route between states does not affect conservation of mass.

options.text: The gas has left the dish, so the mass of it all is unchanged.
options.rationale: Sublimation is a change of state from solid straight to gas, and mass is conserved; the gas has simply left the balance.

mcqs.stem: A 2 kg block of aluminium is cut exactly in half. What is the density of each half?

options.text: The same, because the mass and the volume both halve.
options.rationale: Density is a property of the material. Halving m and V leaves the ratio m / V unchanged.

options.text: Half, because each piece now has only half of the mass.
options.rationale: Only the top of the ratio is tracked; the volume halves at the same time.

options.text: Half, because each piece is lighter than the whole block.
options.rationale: Density is treated as mass, so a lighter piece is assumed to be less dense.

options.text: Double, because the volume of each piece has been halved.
options.rationale: The denominator is halved but the numerator is left alone, so the ratio appears to double.
